newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl keeps Germans guessing about his future.
newsitem.headline: Kohl keeps Germans guessing about his future.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl kept Germans guessing about his future on Thursday as the political rumour mill worked overtime analysing comments by his loyal crown prince that he would like to take over some day.

Kohl told journalists at the start of his annual New Year's news conference there was no need to ask about comments by Wolfgang Schaeuble, which pundits interpreted as a sign the veteran chancellor could step down before the 1998 election.
Schaeuble, the powerful parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), started the speculation by saying he was tempted by the top job but expected Kohl to run next year.
"I do feel temptations, even at my age," Kohl, 66, joked when he was asked the question anyway. "But I am not tempted to answer your question whether I will run or not."

The succession issue arose on Wednesday when Schaeuble, 54, ended years of discretion by telling Stern magazine he felt fit for the job despite the fact he was paralysed from the chest down by a would-be assassin's bullet in 1990.
"Questions about a chancellor in a wheelchair don't bother me," he said. "Helmut Kohl thinks I can do it."
Editorial writers leaped at this as a sign Kohl might step aside in frustration at growing German unemployment to make way for a grand coalition under Schaeuble with the opposition Social Democrats.
Latest data issued on Thursday showed a postwar record with unemployment at 4,156,000 in December.
"Schaeuble has thrown his hat into the ring," said Essen's Westdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung. "This is the first time a CDU politician speaks of himself as a successor to Kohl."
The Stuttgarter Zeitung said: "A pro like Wolfgang Schaeuble weighs his words. So it's clear -- the crown prince is staking his claim, more openly and clearly than ever."
Kohl, who last October became Germany's longest-serving post-war chancellor, has resolutely refused to say whether he will run again in the federal election due in late 1998.

Pundits unanimously agreed that Schaeuble, who served Kohl as chancellery and interior minister before taking over the crucial parliamentary post only a year after being confined to a wheelchair, would not stage a palace coup.
Kohl indirectly underlined this by praising Schaeuble's work, calling him a close friend and choking up slightly when he spoke of the "brutal event" that paralysed him.

RTL Television recalled the CDU's problems with its liberal Free Democratic coalition partners, who have tested Kohl's party by pushing hard for tax cuts without saying how the resulting revenue shortfalls would be financed.
"The CDU's dissatisfaction with the FDP is slowly growing and the mood could swing towards support for a grand coalition," it commented.

Bonn has seen only one CDU-SPD national government, which was formed to win broad support to fight a recession in 1966, and politicians see such "grand coalitions" as a last chance option to deal with major challenges.

"Kohl would not be ready to be chancellor of a grand coalition with the SPD," the Sueddeutsche Zeitung wrote. "That would be Schaeuble's hour, and it could come quickly with these rising unemployment rates and worsening financial problems."

The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung took a more distanced view of the speculation about Schaeuble's comments: "Some people will certainly hear in them a groan under the drudgery of being so loyal to Kohl. But maybe it is only the air escaping from a trial balloon."
